def img(locator,bbox,rationale=None,support='depicted'):
    e={'source_id':D,'locator':locator,'basis':'image','support':support,'bbox':bbox}
    if rationale: e['rationale']=rationale
    return e

def txt(source,locator,quote=None,rationale=None,support='reported'):
    e={'source_id':source,'locator':locator,'basis':'text','support':support}
    if quote:
        assert quote in REG[source]['text'],(source,quote)
        assert len(quote)<=800
        e['quote']=quote
    if rationale: e['rationale']=rationale
    return e

(2012): poly(A)+ RNA, tailed oligo(dT) priming, MMLV/SMART template switching, complementary-strand formation, PCR and purification. The candidate collection page is applicable specifically to its upper figure captioned 'A schematic overview of Smart-Seq.' Its lower Smart-seq2 figure is separate. Smart-seq2 is discussed in surrounding catalogue text but is neither a title target nor an explicitly drawn alternative in the assigned image; no Smart-seq2 chemistry is imported.   'evidence':[page_match,card_smart,smart_input,smart_rt,smart_pcr,card_purify,smart_lib]},
 {'method':'nanoCAGE','operation_ids':[],'status':'resolved',
  'rationale':\"Retained as a distinct target because the card title and method-specific Plessy et al. citation explicitly group nanoCAGE. The paper supports a shared PURPOSE correspondence to the diagram: first-strand reverse transcription, template-switch anchor copying, second-strand priming and amplification. It resolves nanoCAGE itself as random-primed, cap-preferential capture with semi-suppressive PCR and EcoP15I-derived short 5′ tags. That implementation can represent non-polyadenylated RNA. None of the four local operation instances is assigned wholesale to nanoCAGE: each consumes or produces cDNA whose fixed preparation history on this graph is oligo(dT)-primed. Removing o_first from a scope would not change that history at o_second or o_pcr. The paper-supported component correspondence is retained here, while the drawn Smart-Seq route remains intact. The diagram does not depict nanoCAGE tag cleavage, barcoding or its final sequencing library. In nanoCAGE, DNA tags carry captured RNA 5′-end positions for promoter/TSS profiling; template switching preferentially captures capped ends and does not establish perfect cap specificity or that every observed capped end is an original initiation event. Exact local diagram applicability is resolved as a shared principle rather than an identical complete workflow.\",
  'evidence':[txt(C,'Card title, text line 1','Smart-Seq/NanoCAGE/CAGEscan'),card_nano,nano_ts,nano_select,nano_random,nano_pcr,nano_tags,
    txt(NANO,'[b00005], Abstract','Methods that identify the 5′ ends of transcripts will facilitate the discovery of novel promoters and 5′ ends derived from secondary capping events.')]},
 {'method':'CAGEscan','operation_ids':[],'status':'resolved',
  'rationale':\"Retained as a distinct target by the card title and the Plessy et al. citation. CAGEscan shares nanoCAGE's random-primed template-switch capture and its anchor/second-strand/amplification purposes, but uses paired-end-capable cDNA in place of nanoCAGE short-tag cleavage. Its paired DNA reads associate a captured RNA 5′ end with a downstream sequence at the random-priming end; that downstream end is not necessarily the RNA's biological 3′ terminus. CAGEscan can represent poly(A)− RNA. None of this graph's exact local instances is assigned to CAGEscan, because their fixed input/output states have oligo(dT)-primed Smart-Seq preparation history, including the downstream PCR and purification states. This is a resolved correspondence in template-switch principle, not a claim of identical material routes. CAGEscan's distinct final paired-end library interface is not drawn and is not appended as another experimental branch. The paired association can link candidate TSS/promoter regions to downstream transcript features, with cap preference and recapping limitations shared with nanoCAGE.\",

candidate.title: Smart-Seq/NanoCAGE/CAGEscan
candidate.scope: Assigned Illumina grouped card's template-switch cDNA schematic, with the actual drawn poly(A)/oligo(dT) material route resolved to original Smart-Seq cDNA preparation. Inventory: a separate left mRNA/Smart mechanism motif; an A-tailed 'mRNA fragment'; first-strand synthesis by MMLV RT with CCC and an oligo(dT)-linked adaptor; orange-adaptor/second-strand block; paired-strand PCR product; Purify; final DNA. Arrows connect one material route and depict no branches, mixing, cell compartments, sequencing or read-analysis step. The caption-matched upper figure on the candidate collection page specifically identifies Smart-Seq. nanoCAGE and CAGEscan remain distinct grouped title targets with paper-supported correspondence in template-switch capture, while their random-primed implementations are qualified by separate primary-supported local template-switch interfaces and method_scopes, without forcing them onto the oligo(dT)-history states. Those two local interfaces have no drawn branches or material transfer between them; they are paper-supported correspondences only. Their different eventual DNA readout carriers are explained in method_scopes, not reconstructed as complete workflows. SMART template switching is a component, not a fourth workflow. Smart-seq2, discussed alongside a separate schematic in the catalogue, and DLAF and other related-publication assays are outside this assigned image. Purified amplified cDNA is the drawn endpoint; no full Illumina adapter construction is asserted.

states.label: Poly(A)+ mRNA template (source label: 'mRNA fragment')
features: Purple RNA body ending in the depicted A-rich tail; the oligo(dT) interface identifies the tail as the RNA 3′ end.
The isolated left mRNA/Smart motif labels the mechanism. No arrow or operation depicts fragmentation of that motif into this input.
At Smart-Seq implementation scope this is poly(A)+ RNA in total RNA or a cell lysate, not a required prefragmented RNA preparation; no cell compartment is drawn.

states.label: Purified amplified cDNA (final 'DNA' endpoint)
features: The final DNA stroke is schematic simplification after purification; no adapter-cleavage or insert-sequence transformation is depicted.
DNA is the physical carrier of RNA-derived sequence information, not the original RNA. It represents the successfully reverse-transcribed and amplified poly(A)+ RNA population.
This is the depicted cDNA preparation endpoint. The Smart-Seq paper constructs Illumina sequencing libraries from amplified cDNA in subsequent steps; the diagram does not specify that interface.

For Smart-Seq, downstream shotgun sequence coverage supports expression, splice-isoform and expressed-variant analyses; improved full-transcript coverage does not imply complete recovery of every input RNA.
The catalogue describes this Smart-Seq route as not strand-specific; this limitation is not assigned to the distinct nanoCAGE/CAGEscan readouts.

operations.label: First strand synthesis with Moloney murine leukemia virus reverse transcriptase
operations.description: The adaptor-bearing oligo(dT) primer anneals to the poly(A) tail. MMLV reverse transcriptase copies the RNA into complementary first-strand DNA and adds the terminal residues depicted as CCC, producing the RNA/cDNA hybrid shown in the first-strand panel.
operations.mechanism: Tailed oligo(dT) priming and MMLV reverse transcription; terminal transferase activity adds non-templated residues to the first-strand cDNA 3′ end. The enzyme is a catalyst, not a consumed RNA-to-DNA material endpoint.

Smart-seq2 is discussed in surrounding catalogue text but is neither a title target nor an explicitly drawn alternative in the assigned image; no Smart-seq2 chemistry is imported. The endpoint is purified amplified cDNA, not a specification of complete platform-ready library construction.

method_scopes.rationale: Retained as a distinct target because the card title and method-specific Plessy et al. citation explicitly group nanoCAGE. o_nano_template_switch is a separate paper-supported local interface: random-primed cDNA acquires a template-switch-derived anchor for second-strand priming. It captures the shared component purpose illustrated by the grouped diagram without assigning the drawn oligo(dT)-history operation instances to nanoCAGE. The paper resolves nanoCAGE itself as random-primed, cap-preferential capture with semi-suppressive PCR and EcoP15I-derived short 5′ tags, and it can represent non-polyadenylated RNA. The drawn o_first, o_second, o_pcr and o_purify instances remain Smart-Seq-specific: each consumes or produces cDNA with oligo(dT)-primed preparation history. The graph preserves that route and does not append nanoCAGE's complete unshown preparation. Its eventual DNA tags carry captured RNA 5′-end positions for promoter/TSS profiling; template switching does not establish perfect cap specificity or that every capped end marks an original initiation event.

candidate.title: Smart-Seq2
candidate.scope: The assigned Smart-Seq2 schematic, from its depicted poly(A)-tailed mRNA substrate through reverse transcription, LNA-containing template switching, cDNA PCR, tagmentation, and the combined gap-repair/enrichment/purification block to a dual-indexed P5/P7 library fragment. This is a single route without depicted alternatives. The separate Smart-Seq schematic on collection page 97 is not the assigned image. SMART denotes the embedded switching mechanism, not another target assay. Library sequencing and downstream analysis are not separately drawn. The readout interpretation is limited to the resulting RNA-derived indexed DNA library; no pooling, genomic-DNA branch, UMI addition, or additional target workflow is inferred.

The single-cell transcriptome readout samples captured poly(A)+ RNA sequences and their representation through cDNA-derived library inserts. Full-length cDNA supports coverage across transcripts, while each tagmented insert represents only a segment.
The primary protocol abstract states that the method lacks strand specificity and cannot detect poly(A)-negative RNA.
The drawing shows library indices but no UMI or early cell-barcode introduction; it does not establish absolute original RNA molecule counts.

The caption Enrichment-ready fragment is retained literally even though the preceding arrow names enrichment PCR and PCR purification; the graph locates this product after that combined block without adding another enrichment step.
Relative RNA representation can be affected by amplification; the card reports preferential amplification of high-abundance transcripts, so read abundance is not a direct count of starting molecules.

candidate.title: CAGE-Seq
candidate.scope: The assigned Illumina CAGE-Seq schematic: random N15/EcoP15I-primed reverse transcription, RNA biotinylation, RNase-dependent cap trapping, cDNA recovery, and a compressed linker/EcoP15I tag-generation block ending at cDNA. CAGE and cap-analysis gene expression name this target; cap trapping is an embedded selection component. The depicted implementation is clarified by the full-text Takahashi et al. optimized Illumina CAGE protocol (PMID 22362160). The upper and lower molecules contrast incomplete and cap-reaching cDNA outcomes within one workflow. They are neither alternative named methods nor evidence for independent sample splitting or pooling. The left RNA/Cap icon is explanatory context, not a transcription operation. Unshown CAGE adaptations and later library-completion steps are outside this extraction.

features: The drawn substrate is a purple RNA with a black square labeled as the cap and a right-hand AA(A)n tail.

The introductory caption names capped coding and noncoding RNAs as the biological targets. The primary implementation accepts polyadenylated and nonpolyadenylated RNA; the poly(A) drawing does not establish a poly(A)-selection operation.

operations.label: Reverse transcription
operations.description: Prime capped RNA internally with the N15 primer and synthesize complementary DNA toward its 5′ end. operations.mechanism: Reverse transcriptase extends the random primer while retaining the template RNA in an RNA:cDNA hybrid.
operations.information_effect: Transfers RNA sequence into cDNA and introduces a primer-borne EcoP15I site. Only cap-reaching extensions preserve the desired RNA 5′ boundary.

method_scopes.rationale: All recorded operations belong to the one depicted CAGE-Seq implementation; repeated biotinylation, digestion and capture instances preserve branch-specific material histories. The main listed protocol directly supports the N15/EcoP15I architecture. CAGE is the expanded assay name/alias, not an additional target, and cap-trapping remains an Operation component. The drawn AA(A)n substrate does not limit the supported implementation to polyadenylated coding RNA: the figure caption and primary text include capped coding and noncoding RNA and polyadenylated/nonpolyadenylated templates. The selection enriches cap-associated 5′ ends; it is not a complete full-length transcript assay or a direct measure of all nascent initiation. The catalogue reports bias toward TSS of long-lived transcripts. The primary paper states that noncapped RNAs are excluded and very short RNAs may be lost during purification. No equivalence with other CAGE protocols or historical development edge is inferred.

candidate.title: cP-RNA-Seq
candidate.scope: The single cP-RNA-Seq (also styled cP-RNA-seq) chemical-selection and library-construction schematic assigned to this card: extracted RNA with three 3′ end classes → CIP → periodate → T4 PNK → adaptor ligation → RT PCR and purify → cDNA. The three strands are end classes in one RNA population, not alternative assays. The isolated cP-highlighted strand is the title icon. This is the schematic-level implementation clarified by the 2016 protocol, ending at the cDNA library; unshown controls, biochemical validation, optional pretreatments, alternative tRNA-ligase assays and sequencing analysis are outside this graph.

states.label: Extracted RNA: three depicted 3′-end classes
features: Purple RNA strands run 5′ at left to 3′ at right; the top class bears a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (cP), the middle a linear phosphate (P), and the bottom a hydroxyl (OH). The leftmost isolated cP-highlighted strand is a target icon, not another input branch.
The input is an RNA population, not three separately processed samples. The text describes gel-purified RNA of a chosen length entering the chemical selection; the drawing begins at Extracted RNA.
Starting 5′ ends are not assigned individually in the drawing; the primary paper describes a mixture of 5′-P and 5′-OH for these 3′ classes.

operations.description: Treat the extracted RNA mixture with CIP. Remove linear 5′ and 3′ phosphates to yield 5′-OH on all three drawn classes and 3′-OH on the former 3′-P class, while preserving the 3′-cP class.
operations.mechanism: Calf intestine phosphatase (CIP) removes 5′-P and 3′-P but does not remove 3′-cP.
operations.information_effect: The original linear-3′-phosphate and 3′-hydroxyl classes converge to the same chemical substrate for the next selection step; the cP/non-cP distinction is retained.

operations.label: Periodate (NaIO4) treatment
operations.description: Treat the CIP-processed population with periodate. Convert the two 3′-OH classes to the damaged X termini, while the 3′-cP class remains intact.
operations.mechanism: Periodate cleaves the exposed terminal ribose cis-diol to generate 2′,3′-dialdehydes that cannot undergo 3′-adapter ligation. The cP protects the terminal group from this reaction.
operations.information_effect: This creates a differential ligation competence based on the starting 3′ end, rather than physically isolating the top strand. Periodate resistance also occurs for terminal ribose modifications that disrupt the diol, so survival is not a unique assay of cP.

operations.label: Kinase (T4 PNK) treatment
operations.description: Treat the CIP- and periodate-processed population with T4 polynucleotide kinase. Add 5′ phosphate to all drawn classes and remove the surviving cP to produce a 3′-OH on the originally cP-containing RNA; the two X termini remain blocked.
operations.mechanism: T4 PNK removes the 3′-cP and phosphorylates 5′-OH ends, producing the 5′-P/3′-OH substrate required for adapter ligation only in the surviving top class of this drawing.
operations.information_effect: The cP itself is removed, while prior selection is retained in the ability of the original cP class to receive both adapters.

operations.label: Adaptor ligation

candidate.title: RASL-Seq
candidate.scope: The single Illumina RASL-Seq schematic, also captioned A schematic overview of RASL-seq on the verified RNA collection page 11: poly(A)+ RNA -> targeted-probe annealing -> ligation -> displayed streptavidin selection -> probe elution -> indexed DNA library. RASL-Seq and RASL-seq are capitalization aliases for RNA-mediated oligonucleotide annealing, selection and ligation with sequencing. This is a targeted RNA assay whose sequenced carrier is ligated probe-derived DNA. The leftmost highlighted RNA/title graphic is a method emblem, not a separate material route. There are no depicted alternatives, splits or pooling branches. The Li/Qiu/Fu full-text protocol clarifies chemistry and readout; its capture-before-ligation order and probe-derived DNA product are stated explicitly where they differ from the cartoon. Unshown cell-lysate preparation, solid-support alternatives, related assays, kit listings and publication applications do not expand the target scope.

relations.summary: Smart-seq2 retains the Smart-seq template-switching approach while changing the template-switch oligo, reverse-transcription conditions and preamplification.
relations.design_change: Use a 3′ terminal LNA guanylate in the template-switching oligo; add betaine with increased MgCl2; introduce dNTPs before RNA denaturation; use KAPA HiFi preamplification without the intervening first-strand cDNA bead cleanup.

changes.before: The tested commercial SMARTer IIA template-switching oligo.
changes.after: Template-switching oligo terminating in rGrG+G, with +G denoting LNA guanylate.
changes.source_locator: Picelli et al. 2013, PDF p1, first results paragraph and Fig1a.

changes.before: SMARTer-like reverse-transcription buffer with 6 mM MgCl2.
changes.after: Betaine and higher MgCl2 concentrations; dNTPs introduced before RNA denaturation in the optimized procedure.
changes.source_locator: PDF pp1–2, Fig1b–c; Online Methods, Reverse transcription.

changes.before: Bead purification of first-strand cDNA followed by Advantage 2 preamplification.
changes.after: KAPA HiFi preamplification directly after reverse transcription, omitting that intermediate cleanup.
changes.source_locator: PDF p2, paragraph beginning 'The sensitivity and accuracy'; PDF p4, PCR preamplification.

relations.limitation_addressed: Low cDNA recovery, length and transcript detection from single-cell input; an intermediate cleanup also complicates low-volume processing.
relations.reported_gain: The authors report increased cDNA yield/length and improved transcript detection and coverage in their tested settings. Individual modifications and the combined protocol are distinct comparisons; gains must not be assumed additive.
relations.tradeoffs: The paper reports amplification-dependent expression bias and warns that comparisons across amplification procedures can be complicated.

members.explanation: RNA-templated DNA synthesis is combined with stochastic AzNTP termination; the copied product has an intentionally blocked reactive end.
RNA-templated DNA synthesis yields cap-reaching and premature cDNA outcomes; downstream cap trapping treats those outcomes differently.

comparison_groups.summary: Both selected operations copy RNA into DNA by reverse transcription. Their primer architecture, termination behavior and desired products differ; this grouping asserts only that scoped copying mechanism.

comparison_groups.label: Select RNA-origin reporters through terminal features

members.explanation: Differential end treatment makes originally cyclic-phosphate-bearing RNA dual-adapter-ligatable while susceptible other ends remain blocked; the entire sequence is needed to explain the selection.
Copying, biotinylation, RNase protection and capture retain cDNA associated with a capped RNA end. Both successful and rejected molecular outcomes are included; the short branch fails capture.

comparison_groups.summary: Both recover a reporter population determined by an original RNA-end feature. cP-RNA selects through chemical protection and ligatability; CAGE selects cap-associated, 5-prime-complete cDNA through a hybrid/capture route.

comparison_groups.label: Connect reporter sequence to library handles

members.explanation: Chemical adapter joining creates a triazole-linked cDNA template; subsequent PCR depends on polymerase read-through of that junction.
End conversion establishes an adapter-ligatable RNA substrate, then ligation and RT-PCR make a DNA library from dual-adapter-bearing RNA.
The source-level barcoding/P7 block is resolved by the archived primary correction as PCR on ligated DNA probes. Its library is probe-derived, not an RNA-to-cDNA product.

comparison_groups.summary: These connected source blocks give the reporter the handles needed for library amplification, using different substrates and interfaces: click-linked cDNA, enzymatically adapter-ligated RNA, and primer-incorporated handles on a DNA probe reporter.

candidate.title: Drop-Seq
candidate.scope: One Drop-Seq cell/bead droplet implementation repeated in the website diagram and the two selected poster rows. The left yellow-highlighted poly(A) RNA is the biological target; Cell suspension and Each bead with unique oligos are starting materials, not unshown preparation actions. Four bead-primer labels distinguish oligo(dT), molecular index/UMI, cell label and universal handle. The retained route is co-encapsulation → lysis/capture → pooled bead recovery → template-switching cDNA synthesis, PCR and Nextera XT library preparation → sequencing. The output represents captured single-cell mRNA through barcoded 3′-end cDNA tags and UMI-aware digital gene expression. Only the Drop-Seq rows are targets: neighboring CytoSeq, CLaP and Hi-SCL rows, similar-method lists, and review applications do not expand this scope. No separately routed branches appear within the selected rows.

evidence.locator: Left: Single cell with yellow-highlighted RNA and AA(A)n; Cell suspension.
Results [b00009], Drop-Seq steps 2-6.
evidence.quote: Drop-Seq consists of the following steps (Figure 1A): (1) prepare a single-cell suspension from a tissue; (2) co-encapsulate each cell with a distinctly barcoded microparticle (bead) in a nanoliter-scale droplet; (3) lyse cells after they have been isolated in droplets; (4) capture a cell’s mRNAs on its companion microparticle, forming STAMPs (Single-cell Transcriptomes Attached to Microparticles); (5) reverse-transcribe, amplify, and sequence thousands of STAMPs in one reaction; and (6) use the STAMP barcodes to infer each transcript’s cell of origin.

evidence.locator: Left: Single cell with yellow-highlighted RNA and AA(A)n; Cell suspension.
Results [b00011], bead-attached primer orientation and four domains.
evidence.quote: We synthesized oligonucleotide primers directly on beads (from 5’ to 3’, yielding free 3’ ends available for enzymatic priming). Each oligonucleotide is composed of four parts (Figure 1B): (1) a constant sequence (identical on all primers and beads) for use as a priming site for downstream PCR and sequencing; (2) a “cell barcode” (identical across all the primers on the surface of any one bead, but different from the cell barcodes on other beads); (3) a Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) (different on each primer, to identify PCR duplicates) (Kivioja et al., 2012); and (4) an oligo-dT sequence for capturing polyadenylated mRNAs and priming reverse transcription.

evidence.locator: Results [b00017], 3′ digital expression libraries and UMI counting.
evidence.quote: A scientist can then select any desired number of STAMPs for the preparation of 3’-end digital expression libraries (Figure 2C, Experimental Procedures). method_scopes.rationale: All five action blocks apply to the same depicted cell–bead droplet route in all three occurrences. The verified collection heading/description and Macosko full text identify this implementation. evidence.locator: Bead-primer legend reads Oligo dT, Molecular index, Cell label, Universal; neighboring bead icons are captioned Each bead with unique oligos.
Results [b00011], synthesis orientation and four bead-primer domains.
evidence.quote: We synthesized oligonucleotide primers directly on beads (from 5’ to 3’, yielding free 3’ ends available for enzymatic priming). Each oligonucleotide is composed of four parts (Figure 1B): (1) a constant sequence (identical on all primers and beads) for use as a priming site for downstream PCR and sequencing; (2) a “cell barcode” (identical across all the primers on the surface of any one bead, but different from the cell barcodes on other beads); (3) a Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) (different on each primer, to identify PCR duplicates) (Kivioja et al., 2012); and (4) an oligo-dT sequence for capturing polyadenylated mRNAs and priming reverse transcription.

card.description_verbatim:
Drop-Seq analyzes mRNA transcripts from droplets of individual cells in a highly parallel fashion. This single-cell sequencing method uses a microfluidic device to compartmentalize droplets containing a single cell, lysis buffer, and a microbead covered with barcoded primers. Each primer contains: 1) a 30 bp oligo(dT) sequence to bind mRNAs; 2) an 8 bp molecular index to identify each mRNA strand uniquely; 3) a 12 bp barcode unique to each cell and 4) a universal sequence identical across all beads. Following compartmentalization, cells in the droplets are lysed and the released mRNA hybridizes to the oligo(dT) tract of the primer beads. Next, all droplets are pooled and broken to release the beads within. After the beads are isolated, they are reverse-transcribed with template switching. This generates the first cDNA strand with a PCR primer sequence in place of the universal sequence. cDNAs are PCR-amplified, and sequencing adapters are added using the Nextera XT Library Preparation Kit. The barcoded mRNA samples are ready for sequencing.
Similar methods: CEL-Seq, Quartz-Seq, MARS-Seq, CytoSeq, inDrop, Hi-SCL.
advantages_verbatim: Analyze sequences of single-cells in a highly parallel manner
Unique molecular and cell barcodes enables cell and gene specific identification of mRNA strands
Reverse transcription with template-switching PCR produce high-yield reads from single cells
Low cost - $0.07 per cell ($653 per 10,000 cells) and fast library prep (10,000 cells per day)
limitations_verbatim: Requires custom microfluidics device to perform droplet separation
Low gene-per-cell sensitivity compared to other scRNA-Seq methods1

Method Category: Transcriptome > RNA Low-Level Detection
Description: Drop-Seq analyzes mRNA transcripts from droplets of individual cells in a highly parallel fashion. This single-cell sequencing method uses a microfluidic device to compartmentalize droplets containing a single cell, lysis buffer, and a microbead covered with barcoded primers. Each primer contains: 1) a 30 bp oligo(dT) sequence to bind mRNAs; 2) an 8 bp molecular index to identify each mRNA strand uniquely; 3) a 12 bp barcode unique to each cell and 4) a universal sequence identical across all beads. Following compartmentalization, cells in the droplets are lysed and the released mRNA hybridizes to the oligo(dT) tract of the primer beads. Next, all droplets are pooled and broken to release the beads within. After the beads are isolated, they are reverse-transcribed with template switching. This generates the first cDNA strand with a PCR primer sequence in place of the universal sequence. cDNAs are PCR-amplified, and sequencing adapters are added using the Nextera XT Library Preparation Kit. The barcoded mRNA samples are ready for sequencing.
Similar methods: CEL-Seq, Quartz-Seq, MARS-Seq, CytoSeq, inDrop, Hi-SCL.
Pros:
Analyze sequences of single-cells in a highly parallel manner
Unique molecular and cell barcodes enables cell and gene specific identification of mRNA strands
Reverse transcription with template-switching PCR produce high-yield reads from single cells
Low cost - $0.07 per cell ($653 per 10,000 cells) and fast library prep (10,000 cells per day)
Cons:
Requires custom microfluidics device to perform droplet separation
Low gene-per-cell sensitivity compared to other scRNA-Seq methods1
Limited to mRNA transcripts

transitions.before: One RNA preparation containing molecules with different 3-prime ends, depicted as cyclic phosphate, phosphate and hydroxyl.
transitions.change: CIP treatment removes accessible terminal phosphates; cyclic-phosphate-bearing molecules remain a distinct chemical subpopulation.
transitions.after: One treated mixture, not three physically isolated fractions.

evidence.locator: p14 paragraph 2 and first three schematic columns

transitions.before: Treated RNA mixture, including hydroxyl-ended and cyclic-phosphate-ended RNA.
transitions.change: Periodate treatment changes susceptible RNA ends while cyclic-phosphate ends remain protected in this depicted route.
transitions.after: Mixture containing ligation-incompetent oxidized ends and retained cyclic-phosphate ends.

evidence.locator: p14 paragraph 2; Periodate (NaIO4) treatment column

transitions.change: T4 PNK treatment makes the protected class adapter-ligatable; adapters are ligated before RT/PCR.
transitions.after: Adapter-bearing RNA from the selected class, followed by amplified DNA library; the original cyclic phosphate is not retained on the DNA reporter.

evidence.locator: p14 paragraph 2; Kinase treatment through RT-PCR columns

methods.measurement_role: Enrich sequence representation of an RNA population defined by its original 3-prime chemistry.
methods.distinguishing_change: Selection can arise through differential chemical susceptibility and later ligatability, without a physical separation after every reaction.

chemical_drawing_roles.observation: cP/P/OH/X symbols annotate RNA end classes in the workflow; several horizontal molecules coexist.

cross_method_lessons.lesson: A shared library endpoint does not imply a shared measurement mechanism.
examples: ClickSeq creates RNA-derived cDNA fragments; RASL ligates probe reporters; both yield DNA libraries.

cross_method_lessons.lesson: The useful shared unit is a scoped input-change-output relation, including what makes selection/copying/joining possible.
examples: cP-RNA needs original and post-treatment RNA end chemistry.
ClickSeq needs azido terminus and alkyne adapter partner.

cross_method_lessons.lesson: The same physical feature may be biological information, a reagent handle, or an artifact-control device depending on role.
examples: CAGE cap is an original RNA selection feature.
Biotin is a recovery handle across different selected objects.

cross_method_lessons.lesson: Chemical drawings have explicit roles; do not turn a legend molecule into an input or a reaction.
examples: AzNTP is a reagent structure; click-cycloaddition panel is an explicit transformation; biotin/psoralen figures are chemical references.

cross_method_lessons.lesson: A preparation can contain multiple chemical classes without branching the workflow.
examples: Bru-seq labelled and unlabelled RNA before enrichment

cross_method_lessons.lesson: Provenance survives even when the original chemical feature does not.
examples: Cap-selected cDNA is not capped DNA.
cP-selected DNA is not DNA carrying the original RNA cyclic phosphate.

minimal_graph_use.within_method: Represent source-described actions and preparation boundaries; attach specific reactive group, association, sequence/topology and selection-origin claims to the relevant participant. Preserve source grouping unless evidence requires a distinction.
cross_method_candidates: CAGE/TIF: compare use of capped RNA ends, but distinguish selection mechanism and single-end versus paired-end information.
RASL/ClickSeq: compare reporter-construction objectives while keeping probe ligation distinct from RNA copying and chemical adapter joining.
cP-RNA/Bru: compare selection logic, while distinguishing native end chemistry from introduced temporal label.
minimal_graph_use.historical_edges: No historical edge established by this review. Follow explicit cited primary development claims before recording built_on, adapted_from or a corresponding edge.
minimal_graph_use.chemical_encoding: Use supported reactive structures or identifiers at named constituents/groups when needed; symbolic RNA/DNA remainder is allowed. Whole mixed preparation need not have one formula/SMILES.
do_not_infer: Exact reaction conditions from a generic mechanism panel.
Physical separation from multiple molecule lines.
Same mechanism from shared action names or reagent shapes.
A chronological predecessor merely from a shared feature.

examples.observed: Two arrows show cytosine becoming uracil and 5-methylcytosine remaining 5-methylcytosine under the bisulfite-conversion heading.
examples.safe_to_encode: Substrate base identity, depicted conversion/retention and treatment label; link these assertions to the affected DNA base feature when a method row establishes that context.

examples.observed: Separate R-linked drawings identify cytosine, 5-methylcytosine, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine; altered substituents are highlighted.

examples.role: explicit transformation plus matching named workflow row
examples.observed: Sidebar labels an AzNTP structure and copper-catalysed cycloaddition of 3-prime-azido-blocked cDNA to a 5-prime-hexynyl DNA adaptor; the arrow is marked Cu(I) and Rt. The ClickSeq row independently depicts RNA, semi-random primers plus AzNTP/dNTP mixture, purified single-stranded cDNA, click-ligation of an alkyne-modified adaptor, and PCR.
examples.safe_to_encode: The specific terminal handles, cDNA-to-adaptor covalent joining, named catalyst and workflow position. The complementary handles make a much more useful comparison than the word ligation alone.
examples.not_established: Exact oligo sequence, reagent ratio, yield, universal compatibility with other 3-prime blocks, or precedence over another method. Do not expand Rt into a numeric temperature.

examples.example: Acylation followed by DIBO-biotin click labeling

examples.observed: RNA poster shows RNA plus an azide-containing acylating reagent, acylation, then DIBO-biotin click attachment; caption names preparation for biotin-streptavidin purification. DNA poster counterpart labels drawn substrate/products DNA but retains a caption saying RNA.
examples.safe_to_encode: The RNA panel supports an acylation-to-click-labeling sequence and intended affinity-purification role. Preserve the DNA-panel label/caption disagreement as a source-specific conflict.
examples.not_established: Do not silently relabel the DNA panel, infer a DNA/RNA-equivalent reaction, name an attachment nucleotide position, or assign either sidebar to a method merely because it is nearby.

examples.role: reagent/entity references and a labeled class of photoactivatable nucleosides
examples.observed: DNA names pyridostatin. RNA names biotin, psoralen, 4-thiouridine, iodouridine, a bromouridine drawing, thioguanosine, 1,6-hexanediol, Br-UTP and DRB. There are no reaction arrows between these standalone entries.
examples.safe_to_encode: Source names and depicted functional groups for retrieval, with paper-specific role assigned only from a workflow or text. Keep nucleoside and nucleotide-triphosphate forms distinct.
examples.not_established: Not a common protocol or interchangeable ingredient set. The literal labels include 4-bromo uridine (5BrU) and 5-prime-Bromo-uridine (BrdU); verify naming/structure consistency before canonical chemical registration. examples.example: G4-seq supplies the role missing from a reagent legend
examples.role: named reagent connected to a workflow-specific effect
examples.observed: The G4-seq row shows a reference read, removal of the read fragment, renewed primer hybridization, addition of K+ or PDS to stabilize G4 regions, a second read with polymerase stalls, and comparison of reads.
examples.safe_to_encode: PDS is a reagent option at a particular operation with the source-stated stabilization effect; contrast conditions and observed readout matter as well as chemical identity.
examples.not_established: The PDS structure alone does not establish this role, nor does common PDS usage establish that two methods are descendants or interchangeable.

examples.observed: First cDNA synthesis uses a dTTP-containing nucleotide mixture; second-strand synthesis is labeled with dUTP and the corresponding strand carries U symbols. The amplification panel marks that strand with Block polymerase.
examples.safe_to_encode: Which strand acquires uracil, at which copying operation, and the depicted consequence during amplification. A generic DNA state would lose the differentiating information.
examples.not_established: Do not fill in an unshown enzyme identity or an unshown uracil-removal reaction from familiarity with other stranded RNA-seq protocols.

examples.example: TruSeq RNA Access and Nextera Library Preparation
examples.role: non-equivalent uses of broad workflow operations
examples.observed: RNA Access depicts biotinylated target probes hybridized to library targets, streptavidin magnetic-bead capture and elution. Nextera depicts adaptor-loaded transposase acting on DNA, tagmentation and amplification.
examples.safe_to_encode: Capture through a probe-associated biotin tag differs from direct molecular biotinylation; tagmentation combines fragmentation and adaptor introduction within the depicted block.
examples.not_established: Shared words such as capture or adaptor addition do not establish the same transformation, identical linkage chemistry, or historical inheritance.

conclusion: The posters mix molecular structures, schematic transformations, workflow context and navigation artwork. They should not all become operation nodes.

Record a chemical entity/feature separately from what a particular operation does to it. A useful operation comparison includes substrate features, action, resulting features, attachment relationship and readout consequence where depicted.

Several technologies share preparation or readout stages while differing in one selective chemical operation, the stage at which a tag is attached, or which strand/fraction retains the tag. This is an observed comparison strategy, not a universal fixed chain.
Chemical structure or formula can improve identification of specific reagents and reactive handles, but cannot replace molecule association, compartment, barcode attribution or operation order.

Cross-method correspondence may compare these evidenced transformations. Evolutionary edges still need the paper-specific claim of adoption/change and the older source; no historical edge is established by this review.
review_limits: Source drawings are simplified and may contain caption/label errors.
No SMILES, InChI, molecular formula or atom-mapped reaction was inferred from an image.
No new ontology/schema code, native model calls, or canonical method connections were created.
